items.title: 5.8 Homogeneous Equation of the Second Degree in Two Variables

source_refs.note: Book p. 159 (PDF 161, upper part): pair of lines, joint equation (iii), general second degree equation (iv), lines y = m1 x, y = m2 x and their joint equation (v)

blocks.text: We know that if a graph is a straight line in a plane, then its equation is a linear equation in two variables \(x\) and \(y\). Conversely, the graph of any linear equation in \(x\) and \(y\) is a straight line.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: A linear equation has degree 1: every term is a number, a number times \(x\), or a number times \(y\), as in \(2x - 3y + 5 = 0\). No \(x^{2}\), no \(xy\), no \(y^{2}\). Such an equation always draws a straight line, and every straight line has such an equation. In this section we join TWO lines into ONE equation, and that single equation turns out to have degree 2.

Suppose we have two straight lines represented by
\[a_{1}x + b_{1}y + c_{1} = 0 \quad \text{...(i)}\]
and
\[a_{2}x + b_{2}y + c_{2} = 0 \quad \text{...(ii)}\]

Multiplying equations (i) and (ii), we have
\[(a_{1}x + b_{1}y + c_{1})\times\]
\[(a_{2}x + b_{2}y + c_{2}) = 0 \quad \text{...(iii)}\]
It is a second degree equation in \(x\) and \(y\).

Equation (iii) is called joint equation of the pair of lines (i) and (ii). On the other hand, given an equation of second degree in \(x\) and \(y\), say
\[ax^{2} + 2hxy + by^{2}\]
\[+\, 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 \quad \text{...(iv)}\]
where \(a \ne 0\) represents equations of a pair of lines if (iv) can be resolved into two linear factors. In this section, we shall study special joint equations of pairs of lines which pass through the origin.
bold: joint equation of the pair of lines

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does multiplying work? A product is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero (the zero-product rule). So a point \((x, y)\) satisfies (iii) exactly when it satisfies (i) or (ii), that is, when it lies on one of the two lines. One equation now describes both lines together; that is why it is called their joint equation.
Why degree 2? Each bracket has degree 1; multiplying an \(x\)-term by an \(x\)-term gives \(x^{2}\), an \(x\)-term by a \(y\)-term gives \(xy\), and so on.
Our example: the lines \(x - y = 0\) and \(x + y = 0\) have the joint equation \((x - y)(x + y) = 0\), that is \(x^{2} - y^{2} = 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The other direction needs care: not every second degree equation is a pair of lines. For example \(x^{2} + y^{2} - 1 = 0\) is a circle; it cannot be split into two linear factors with real coefficients. That is why the book says (iv) represents a pair of lines only IF it can be resolved into two linear factors.
In (iv) the middle term is written \(2hxy\) (and \(2gx\), \(2fy\)) with a 2 in front. This is only a convention that makes later formulas neater, for example \(h^{2} - ab\) in Theorem 8.

Let \(y = m_{1}x\) and \(y = m_{2}x\) be two lines passing through the origin. Their joint equation is:
\[(y - m_{1}x)(y - m_{2}x) = 0\]
or
\[y^{2} - (m_{1}+m_{2})xy + m_{1}m_{2}x^{2} = 0 \quad \text{...(v)}\]
Equation (v) is a special type of a second degree homogeneous equation.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How does (v) come out? Expand the brackets:
\[(y - m_{1}x)(y - m_{2}x)\]
\[= y^{2} - m_{2}xy - m_{1}xy + m_{1}m_{2}x^{2}\]
\[= y^{2} - (m_{1}+m_{2})xy + m_{1}m_{2}x^{2}\]
Look at (v): every term has total degree exactly 2 (\(y^{2}\), \(xy\), \(x^{2}\)); there is no \(x\)-term, no \(y\)-term and no constant. This is what 'homogeneous' means, and it happens because both lines pass through the origin: putting \(x = 0, y = 0\) must give 0.
Also notice: the coefficient of \(xy\) is minus the SUM of the slopes, and the coefficient of \(x^{2}\) is the PRODUCT of the slopes (when the coefficient of \(y^{2}\) is 1). We use this in 5.9.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. The joint equation of two lines is the product of their equations set equal to zero.
2. Two linear equations multiplied give a second degree equation in \(x\) and \(y\).
3. A second degree equation (iv) is a pair of lines only when it splits into two linear factors.
4. Two lines through the origin \(y = m_{1}x\), \(y = m_{2}x\) have joint equation (v), in which every term has degree 2 (homogeneous).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Adding the two equations instead of multiplying them. \((x - y) + (x + y) = 0\) gives \(x = 0\), a single line, not the pair. Only the product keeps both lines.
Thinking every second degree equation is a pair of lines: \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 1\) is a circle.
